tables.how: The Bay Area hospices in Medicare's yearly provider file whose payments in their latest year were $1 million or more and at least ten times their first year on record, ranked by that multiple; the case counts the first eight, and this list gives every year in which each was paid. The eight latest-year rows add up to $39,967,262, the case's figure; the eight first-year rows add up to $1,548,121. 4 more hospices meet the same test and are in the next list. Paid per person is the year's payment divided by the people served that year.
tables.limits: Growth from a small first year is large by arithmetic: a new agency starts near zero, and its first year on record may be a part year. Agencies also grow by buying another agency or by winning referral agreements with hospitals and nursing homes. Medicare pays hospice a daily rate, so payment follows days of care; the file shows no diagnoses and cannot show whether anyone was wrongly enrolled. No authority has acted against any hospice listed. No row shows fewer than 11 people served: the download's notes say federal payment files withhold counts under 11, so a hospice's smallest years may be missing. People served in two years are counted in each.

tables.how: All 121 hospice records in the project's Bay Area extract that show a Medicare payment in 2018 to 2024. The screen keeps a hospice paid $1 million or more in its latest year if that is at least four times its first year and no more than four years later, or if its State licence is dated 2020 or later: 25 hospices. 12 of them grew ten-fold or more; the case counts the first eight by multiple. The other 96 are listed so the eight can be set against everyone else.
tables.limits: The licence date is blank where the download could not tie a State licence to the Medicare record by a shared number, so some hospices licensed since 2020 are not marked. A hospice whose latest paid year is before 2024 has stopped billing under that number, which can mean a sale or a new number and not a closure. The ordinary reasons for fast growth in the first list apply to every row here.

tables.how: Each of the eight hospices was looked up by its Medicare enrollment number in the newest quarterly Hospice All Owners file that holds it (7 in the file dated 2026-10-01; 1 in the file dated 2026-04-01). Every row with an ownership, partner, director, officer or managerial-control role is listed, so one person can appear once for each role. 15 rows that name a person only as a managing employee are left out: they are staff, not owners. The owner's number is the federal file's own identifier, which is what ties one owner to several agencies; none of these numbers appears under two or more of the eight hospices.
tables.limits: This is what each hospice told Medicare, not a finding about anyone named. Owning or running a hospice whose payments grew quickly is not evidence of wrongdoing, and the case's own text says ownership links were not analysed. A name in this list is not shown to be the same person as anyone of that name in another record. Shares are as reported and need not add up to 100%. The file does not show who owned a hospice before April 2023.

tables.how: The case says the test of fast growth lies in how long people stay and how many leave hospice alive. The download holds the State's yearly utilization reports, so each of the eight was looked up there: 6 of 8 have at least one report, 25 report-years in all. Where the download had already joined the State and Medicare records by a shared number that join is used; otherwise a State record is shown only when both its name and its street address match, and the row says the tie is not confirmed. A blank cell is a blank in the State file.
tables.limits: These are the hospice's own yearly totals, unaudited, and several hospices skipped years (shown in the last-but-one column). A rising count of people who leave alive or stay beyond 180 days has ordinary causes: a prognosis is an estimate, and people move away or choose treatment again. The State and Medicare count different years (the State by report period) and different payers, so the two lists do not reconcile to the day. No hospice with no State report on disk can be judged at all.
tables.of: The download holds a State report for only some of the eight hospices and some of the years; the others filed none that could be tied to the Medicare record.
